note: Apollo and Diana, the twin children of the goddess Latona: the sun and the moon.

quote: the sun crowned by the Ram, the moon by the Scales
note: The sun is in Aries and the full moon opposite it in Libra, as happens around the spring equinox. At sunset the two sit on opposite horizons, one sinking as the other rises. They are level for an instant only.

The sun and moon are on the horizon, not overhead. In Dante's image the zenith, the point straight above, is the hand that holds the scales, with the sun in one pan and the moon in the other. The balance lasts a single moment, and that is how long Beatrice pauses.
God, seen as a point of blinding light ringed by nine circles of angels (Canto 28).

quote: where every When and Where converges
note: In God, for whom all places are here and all times are now. Beatrice reads Dante's questions there. They are about the angels: where, when and how they were made.

quote: Not to gain anything for himself
note: Why God created. He lacked nothing and could gain nothing. He created out of love, so that other beings could share in existence and reflect his light back.
Dante uses one Latin word, "Subsisto": I exist, I stand as a being in my own right. Creation gives God's reflected light a life of its own.
The angels, who are called Loves throughout these cantos. Some readers take the phrase more widely, as everything God made.
Time began with creation, so it makes no sense to ask what God was doing beforehand. Augustine makes the same argument in his Confessions.
From the second verse of Genesis: "the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters".

Terms from Aristotle. Matter is the stuff a thing is made of, and form is what makes it the kind of thing it is. God made three things at once: pure form (the angels), pure matter (the raw stuff of the world below), and the two joined (the heavens).
An imagined bow that shoots three arrows in one shot, for the three things made in one act.
Creation took no time. Light fills a clear glass the instant it arrives, and so angels, heavens and matter came to be together, in one flash.
In Aristotle's terms, "act" is what a thing fully is, and "potential" what it could become. Angels are pure act: nothing in them is unfinished or waiting to develop.
Bare matter is nothing definite in itself, but can become anything once it receives a form.
Usually taken as the heavens: matter and form joined so perfectly that they can never decay or come apart, unlike things on earth.

context: Jerome thought the angels were made long ages before the rest of the world. Thomas Aquinas disagreed, with respect, and Dante sides with Aquinas: everything was created together.

note: The writers of the Bible. Commentators point to the first verse of Genesis, "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth", and to Ecclesiasticus 18:1, which says God "created all things together".
The angels turn the heavens: that is part of what they are for. Had they been made ages before the heavens, they would have gone all that time with nothing to move.
Dante's three unspoken questions about the angels: where they were created, when, and how.

quote: Before you could count to twenty
note: The rebel angels fell almost the moment they were made. Theologians debated how long the interval was. Dante makes it a few seconds.

The earth, the lowest of the four elements of which everything under the moon was thought to be made: earth, water, air and fire. The falling angels struck it. Inferno 34 tells how the land fled from Lucifer as he fell.
The circling dance around God that Dante saw in Canto 28. It is the angels' whole occupation and their joy.

context: Dante saw him at the bottom of Hell, fixed at the center of the earth, the point toward which every weight in the universe presses (Inferno 34).

note: The good angels acknowledged that they owed their being and their great minds to God. Lucifer's sin was to refuse this.

quote: enlightening grace and their own merit
note: The loyal angels were rewarded with the full sight of God. It fixed their wills on him for good, so they can no longer sin.

quote: it is worthy to receive this grace
note: Grace is a gift, but accepting it is an act of the will, and so deserves reward. The more open the heart, the more is given.
The universities, where theology was taught by lecture and formal debate.

Dante's Italian says that the angel "understands, remembers and wills": the three powers Augustine found in the human mind. Beatrice's objection is to memory. Remembering means calling back something no longer in view, and the angels never look away from God, in whom they see everything at once.
The teachers who say otherwise. Some believe their own errors. Others know better and teach them anyway, which is worse.
The wish to look clever and original. It sends philosophers off in every direction instead of down the one road of truth.
The blood of Christ, and of the apostles and martyrs who died spreading the Gospel.

A theory to explain the darkness at the Crucifixion as an eclipse. Christ died at Passover, at full moon, when the moon is on the far side of the earth from the sun. So some said it miraculously ran back to stand in front of the sun.
Beatrice's reply: an eclipse darkens only part of the earth, but this darkness covered all of it. The sun must have dimmed itself.
The western and eastern ends of the inhabited world as Dante knew it, with Jerusalem at the middle.

context: Lapo and Bindo, short forms of Jacopo and Aldobrando, were among the commonest men's names in the city.

note: The congregation, Christ's flock, goes home from the sermon having been given nothing. Beatrice adds that their ignorance does not excuse them: they should know empty talk when they hear it.

quote: 'Go preach idle tales to the world,'
note: A bitter twist on Christ's command to the apostles: "Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature" (Mark 16:15).
The hood of a friar's habit. The preaching orders, Franciscans and Dominicans, are the main target.
The devil. Dante's Italian says "such a bird" nests in the point of the hood. Devils were often pictured with wings, as the angels are.

Indulgences: the church's remission of the punishment still owed for sins already confessed. Only proper authority could grant them. Beatrice says preachers hand them out with no authority at all, and the crowd asks for no proof.

Anthony the Abbot, the Egyptian hermit of the third and fourth centuries who is honored as the father of monks. Art shows him with a pig at his feet. The monks of his order kept pigs that roamed the towns and were fed by the public out of piety. Beatrice says the monks fatten themselves the same way.
Usually taken to be the monks' hangers-on, mistresses and illegitimate children, kept on the proceeds.
The false pardons, given in exchange for real offerings. Dante's phrase is money with no stamp on it: coin that no mint has made good.
Beatrice admits the digression and goes back to the angels. Time is short: only four cantos remain.

context: In his vision of God's throne, "thousand thousands ministered unto him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him" (Daniel 7:10). Beatrice says these figures stand for a number beyond human counting, not an exact sum.

note: God. Every angel receives his light in its own way and to its own degree, so no two angels see him, or love him, quite alike.

quote: affection follows the act of understanding
note: The rule from Canto 28: seeing comes first and love follows. Each angel loves God as much as it sees of him.
The angels. God's one light is reflected in countless separate mirrors, and yet it is not divided or lessened.
